awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Bridging Multi-Party Computation and Fully Homomorphic Encryption for Practical Data Security Solutions
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will result from the development of a novel data security technology that enables organizations to collaboratively analyze data in encrypted form, in turn providing the strongest data privacy and security guarantees.  This innovation addresses the growing need for secure data processing in sectors like healthcare, finance, and government, where sensitive information must be protected during computation. The proposed solution combines two powerful cryptographic techniques - Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) and Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) - to create a unified protocol that balances computational efficiency with strong privacy guarantees. By reducing the high computational and communication overheads associated with existing methods, the technology makes privacy-preserving computation more accessible and scalable for real-world applications. This advancement has the potential to significantly impact how organizations collaborate and extract insights from sensitive data while complying with data protection regulations. It will also promote public trust in the use of artificial intelligence and data-driven technologies by ensuring that privacy is preserved throughout the computational process.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project aims to develop and evaluate a new cryptographic protocol called McFHE that efficiently combines the strengths of FHE and MPC. The core challenge addressed by this project is the impracticality of current privacy-preserving computation methods when applied to large-scale datasets. The research will focus on designing the McFHE protocol, building foundational operations such as dot products and comparisons, and evaluating its performance in practical applications like privacy-preserving machine learning. A custom software library will be developed to integrate these cryptographic techniques and assess their computational, communication, and memory requirements. The project also includes a real-world use case involving secure training of AI models on medical imaging data. Anticipated results include a working prototype of the McFHE system and performance benchmarks that demonstrate its viability for commercial deployment. This work lays the foundation for broader adoption of privacy-preserving technologies in sensitive and regulated industries.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The rapid adoption of cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for innovation across industries. However, it has also introduced important challenges related to data privacy, security, and confidentiality. Organizations in healthcare, finance, government, and other sectors increasingly rely on cloud-based computing to analyze sensitive information, often requiring data to be exposed during processing.

This NSF Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project, conducted by CipherSonic Labs, focused on developing technologies that enable organizations to perform useful computations on sensitive information while maintaining its confidentiality throughout the process.

Intellectual Merit and Scientific Outcomes

The primary objective of the project was to investigate and demonstrate the feasibility of a novel privacy-preserving computing framework called McFHE, which combines two advanced cryptographic techniques: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) and Secure Multiparty Computation (MPC).

FHE enables computations to be performed directly on encrypted data without requiring decryption. MPC allows multiple parties to collaborate on computations without revealing their individual private information. Although both technologies offer important privacy protections, their practical adoption has historically been constrained by computational complexity and communication requirements.

The research explored how these complementary technologies could be integrated to improve the efficiency and practicality of secure computation.

Over the course of the project, the research team successfully designed and implemented the McFHE framework and developed foundational computational capabilities needed for privacy-preserving data analytics and machine learning.

The team also developed an experimental software framework based on OpenFHE, an established open-source cryptographic library, to support hybrid privacy-preserving computation.

The developed technologies were evaluated through experimental benchmarking and cloud-based prototype demonstrations. The results demonstrated the technical feasibility of the proposed approach and showed promising improvements in computational and communication efficiency compared with conventional methods.

The research also provided valuable insights into the architectural and system-level challenges associated with performing complex computations on encrypted data. These findings establish a foundation for further advances in scalable and efficient privacy-preserving computing.

Broader Impacts and Potential Applications

The outcomes of this project have potential applications across a wide range of industries where protecting sensitive information is essential.

In healthcare, privacy-preserving computation could support secure analysis of medical information and enable collaboration among organizations while reducing risks associated with exposing confidential patient records.

In financial services, these technologies could support fraud detection, risk assessment, and collaborative analytics while protecting sensitive customer and business information.

Similar capabilities could benefit government agencies, research institutions, and enterprises that need to analyze or share information while maintaining strict confidentiality.

As an additional outcome, the project explored the application of privacy-preserving computation to modern artificial intelligence systems and developed a prototype demonstrating encrypted AI inference in a cloud environment. This work highlighted opportunities to enable organizations to benefit from AI technologies while maintaining greater control over sensitive information.

The project also contributed to the development of interdisciplinary expertise in applied cryptography, secure computing, cloud infrastructure, and privacy-preserving AI. Research findings and prototype demonstrations were shared with relevant technical and industry stakeholders.

Overall Project Outcomes

The NSF SBIR Phase I project successfully demonstrated the scientific and technical feasibility of integrating complementary cryptographic technologies to support efficient privacy-preserving computation.

The resulting research findings, software capabilities, and prototype demonstrations provide a foundation for future innovation in secure data analytics, confidential cloud computing, and privacy-preserving artificial intelligence.

By advancing technologies that reduce the need to expose sensitive information during computation, this research contributes toward a future in which organizations can benefit from advanced computing and AI while maintaining strong protections for data privacy and confidentiality.
